utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, July 8th, 2009, and I greet Mr. Praljak first and foremost, then Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic. Of course I would like us to think about Mr. Coric. I also welcome our Defence counsels, Mr. Stringer and his associate, our Registrar, and everyone helping us, including our Usher. The Coric Defence cross-examination will continue, the cross-examination of Mr. Praljak, and I give the floor to Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Tomasegovic Tomic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Praljak. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're looking at the third binder and that's where we're starting today. Here is where we left off yesterday, Mr. Praljak. I have no intention of calling the document again. There's no need to waste time on that. We were looking at the structure of the HVO military police dated the 26th of June -- the 26th of December, 1992. We were going through that structure document, and I was showing you the portion that says that the commanders of the battalions of the military police with the OZs in the execution of their daily tasks were directly subordinated to the operations zone commander and were carrying out any orders in relation to the execution of military police tasks, and in compliance with the authority and competencies of the military police. The document was P00957. You remember now what we were talking about and what you said. I hope I don't have to go through it all again. May we first -- please look at the first document in this binder, that's P01344. The date is the 29th of January, 1993, the number is 01-185/93. These are instructions for further work. Chief of the Main Staff, Mr. Petkovic, sent this to Mr. Siljeg, who was in the Prozor-based branch of the HVO. Can we please go to paragraph 7 of this document which reads: "Station responsible police patrols at the exit from Vakuf and the entrance to Prozor to arrest looters from our side, detain them, and confiscate their plunder." Mr. Praljak, can you please tell me whether what I've just read back to you, I mean police patrols and arresting looters as well as detaining them and confiscating their loot, is something that was part of the military police business?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] May we please move on to the next document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, could you please read out loud paragraph 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quote: "Arrest and imprison all our extremists."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Arrest and imprison all our extremists. What exactly does this mean -- at least what did this mean in January 1993? First, as far as extremists were concerned, was this the Muslim extremists or was this all Muslims on all sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ours, the Croat ones.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: All --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who had a different view vis-a-vis the policies that were in favour of restoring peace and restoring amicable relations with the BH army. There were people who were at odds with that policy and advocated the view that the HVO should, in fact, launch an attack and that such a policy will lead us down an alley where we might end up losing every single battle. Their arguments were not entirely without merit. Not everything they said stood for extremist viewpoints, but here Petkovic requested that they all be eliminated and I was in favour of that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, any reasonable trier of fact reading this paragraph could read it in two different ways. First, Mr. Petkovic is instructing Siljeg to arrest all those who do not share the same political line as the HVO, whether it's a civilian or military component. I'm not going to get into that. And thus consequently all people who, according to the Prosecution's case, would not participate in the enterprise carried out. First reading. The second reading that any reasonable trier of fact could have, of course taking into account all elements in the file and in the case, Mr. Petkovic is asking Siljeg to arrest all trouble-makers, all those who are acting against peace or intervening against the cease-fire and who are acting against those who want to make the Vance-Owen Plan a success. Now, those are two different readings. Now, according to your answer I believe that you would interpret this in the second way; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On page 3, line 14, replace "Muslims on all sides" with "extremists on all sides."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they're interlinked, the two things are. On the 22nd, or rather, the 23rd of January, 1992, the HVO inflicted a military defeat on the BH army in Gornji Vakuf and was holding all of the important elevations. At this point in time, I asked Siljeg, or rather, told Siljeg now that the objective of our operation had been reached to withdraw the BH army and lift the siege around the HVO, given, however, the number of those killed and wounded a military man's thinking went along the lines of taking Vakuf next, which is a very strong impulse, exceptionally strong. One has to stand up to something like that because this was not within the framework of the HZ HB policy, the policy espoused by all of us. So I said no. The objective of lifting the blockade had been accomplished and we were no longer launching attacks. Nevertheless, what do you tell these same people six months later? This was the policy pursued in Bugojno, in Konjic, and everywhere else, and then those people who spoke differently back then come back to you to tell you, So General what about it now, look what at what they did to us in Bugojno, and Look at how they betrayed us in Mostar, and so on and so forth. In other words, the implementation of political decisions, whenever these decisions are at odds with the situation on the ground and any information being received is not an easy thing to do, particularly because decisions like that are paid in blood, enormous amounts of blood, and deaths, dozens and dozens of those who get killed and wounded in an operation like that. And then they'll come back to tell you we could have taken Uskoplje, we could have taken control of Bugojno, whereas now because of all this we have lost both. 15.000 of our people have been expelled from [as interpreted] Rama alone. Next thing up, Doljani on the 28th of July, 63 Croats were killed. You've got to stand up to this. You have to do something about the emotional desperation, that is actually technical term that these people feel. Your Honours, now that I've been talking about this, some time late in July 1993, let's say there's someone in Rama, say me, and I'm a member of the joint criminal enterprise, after what happened in Bugojno, after what happened in Mostar, and then we know what happened in Doljani later on where 63 people were killed on the 28th of July, I gave a single speech, for example, or allowed someone else to give a speech telling other people something along the lines of, Look at what they're doing to us. We would have seen massive acts of retaliation with hundreds of Muslims killed. In reality, the number of undesirable incidents was kept down to a minimum I might say, precisely because this emotional fire was eventually put out due to exceptional efforts made by a number of people, including me. It is not necessarily legal category but you have this desperation that people feel, even law provides for that come to speak of it. In the case of manslaughter, for example, or when insanity is pled, and this is what happened in that month over there. It's very difficult for me to explain exactly what the situation was like and then we call them extremists, but they came back to us to say, It's not that we're extremists, you are idiots because we were advocating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please be brief. Your answer is much too long. We've understood what you want to convey. I give the floor to Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I called the next document already, P01359. The document is signed by the commander of the operations zone, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. The document is dated the 30th of January, 1993, addressed to three different brigades as well as all the units in the Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Bugojno areas. The title is: "Taking measures in the units - order." The first sentence reads: "Pursuant to an order from the Chief of the HVO Main Staff 01-185/93, dated the 29th of January, 1993 ..." Mr. Praljak, can we pause there for a moment. Look at the previous document and that appears to be that very order; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one that Mr. Siljeg invokes here. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Can we now please go to paragraphs 11, 13, and 16 of this same document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, Mr. Siljeg says: "The military police will establish full control of the people and goods entering or leaving the Gornji Vakuf area and will also arrest individuals or groups acting in contravention of this order as well as any previous ones. Individuals in any of the units will be brought to the forward command post in Prozor for disciplinary measures to be imposed." Paragraph 13 reads: "The SIS and military police shall arrest any looters, bring them in, seize and record any stolen goods, and oppose any resistance to the implementation of this order." Now we come to paragraph 16, and Mr. Siljeg says that this order should be copied and sent out to all the commanders up to the level of platoon, and that all the soldiers should be informed about this, and is requesting that he be informed of the implementation of the order. Now, tell me, these paragraphs, 11 and 13, do they refer to the military police and its duties, because we have the control of the entrance and exit of goods, the arrest of people who have stolen and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you have paragraph 12 as well -- but anyway, the SIS and security organs must work along these lines in the course of carrying out their duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next document, P01548 is the number of the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, this document by Mr. Siljeg is the logical follow-up of order that was previously given by General Petkovic, there's actually a reference to it. But what surprises me - and I would like you to give us your opinion - is that we find out that Colonel Siljeg is somewhat adding as relates to the political situation, he's adding things. I'm sure you have noted on paragraph 9, for example, there is reference to what might have been -- all the actions that might have been carried out again, UNPROFOR, the Red Cross, and so forth. So I would like to know whether in the HVO it was normal practice for the subordinates to supplement the original order and go a bit beyond the original order by adding their own personal views on the events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is customary, Your Honour, for the commander of the operations zone of at least divisional rank, so he's not a sergeant or anything like that, he has a high rank and performs a high military duty, and he's there in the territory, on the ground, and of course his order must not be in contravention and opposed to the orders issued by the Chief of the Main Staff. But he is allowed to elaborate and that is, in fact, necessary and required, adjusting it to the situation on the ground as he knows it. Because he knows the situation on the ground better than General Petkovic, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to call up document P01548, which is the next document, and it is a document from Mr. Siljeg. The date of the document is the 25th of February, 1993, and it is addressed to the brigades, one from Bugojno, one from Vakuf. The document is titled: "Engagement of Forces for the Execution of Military Police Tasks in Gornji Vakuf." Now, Mr. Praljak, first of all let's take a look at the middle of the next paragraph before the order, the actual order. It says: "Since the forces of the HVO from Livno, Tomislavgrad, Posusje, and Prozor have participated in combat actions in Gornji Vakuf, it would be very risky to engage the military police manpower from those areas in tasks in Gornji Vakuf. Since the military police quite recently has been subordinated to the brigades commands and OZ, operation zones, for the purpose of adequate engagement and establishment ..." et cetera, et cetera. Let's just discuss this part where Mr. Siljeg says where most recently the VP has been subordinated to the brigade commands and the OZ, and we see that the date of the document is the 25th of February, 1993. I don't know what Mr. Siljeg means when he says "most recently," but all I can say is that it was before the 25th of February, 1993. Now, Mr. Praljak, I stopped here because yesterday you said in response to a question from Judge Antonetti recorded on page 97 and 98 of the transcript for that day -- well, you said the following, and I'm going to read it out in English to avoid any misunderstanding. [In English] "Up until the point in time when the situation on the battle-field become very bad for the HVO, and that was even prior to my arrival, and at the time of my arrival, the military police had not been involved in any combat operations. I then sought and received those powers. As of such time, a commander, me or anyone else, was in position to use military police on a combat mission." [Interpretation] Now the reasons for which I read this out are the following. From the order by Colonel Siljeg, one can understand it differently than what you said yesterday. Do you understand where the problem is, the problem is in time, in the period of time, and can you explain us then why there's this difference and do you see the difference that I'm trying to point out? Do you understand what I'm trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct something, or rather, be more precise in my statement. The military police before - and I'm asking -- I'm talking about the time when I ask that it be engaged - but even before that the military police could take part in combat action to the best of my knowledge; however, you had to ask permission from the chief of the military police. And generally speaking -- well, with my arrival I would not have asked any changes in the way the military police can be deployed by enabling me to engage the military police without previously having asked permission from Mr. Coric, the chief of the military police. So that's the additional explanation that I wish to give now. Secondly, I don't know on what grounds this order -- well, when it says "most recently," I don't know what that means and why Siljeg didn't specify. So I can't comment on that because in order to do so I would have to see the order by which the way in which the military police was involved and engaged was changed. And thirdly, had I known that this was the case, it would -- there would be no logic to me seeking permission and receiving permission from Mate Boban to be allowed to use the military police without having gained permission from the chief of the military police, which was Mr. Coric. So that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I apologise for running ahead of the transcript. Mr. Praljak, you've just told us about combat operations and action, but let's look at the document further down because I think what it says further down does not relate to the engagement of the military police in combat operations. So let me read once again. It says: "Since the military police from a certain time was subordinated to the brigade commands and OZ, operations zones, and for the purpose of adequate engagement and establishment of order in Gornji Vakuf -- in the Gornji Vakuf territory, all the more so since the situation threatens that the BH army might assign its own police at check-points and thereby unilaterally block all communications on the Gornji Vakuf territory, thereby cutting off the existing HVO units. And for the purpose of preventing such a situation, I hereby order ..." And then he goes on to say in point 1: "The Eugen Kvaternik Brigade will secure 25 military policemen or other units for the execution of the military police tasks at the check-point and shall inform the forward command post of the OZ of the north-western Herzegovina area in Prozor and will also inform the commander of the brigade." Now, Mr. Praljak, as far as I understand this order, Mr. Siljeg refers 20 military police tasks here, and then he refers to the fact that the military police from a certain -- for a certain amount of time was subordinated to the brigade commands of the OZ, and he issues orders stating what's going to happen with the check-points. So he's dealing with military police matters and not combat operation matters. Am I right in understanding it that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Siljeg is asking is that the military police - and it's right to do so - he's asking the military police to perform its duties. That's very simple. He's not dealing with military police tasks or whatever because the military police has been established in the way it has, it cannot replace the commander, he does not provide the salaries, they have their structure, write reports, and so on. He says here quite simply - and that's his right - that he demands that the military police goes about its military police duties in the way in which he considers that they should do on the territory where he is the commander in order to help establish peace and there's nothing illogical there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, Mr. Siljeg isn't addressing the military police here. He's addressing the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade and telling them to secure the military police in the performance of their duties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because you can't address the military police if it's coming down from the top, if he's asking permission, this would disrupt the system. The system has to act quickly and urgently. It was a very slow system and couldn't actually be used, so the commander can ask the military police to carry out its military police duties without having to receive permission every time from the chief of the military police himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, yesterday we were looking at the establishment documents of the military police, P00957 was the number. Now, is it possible that Mr. Siljeg was referring back to those -- that establishment document and that's where he reaps his rights from subordinate to the -- in the organisational sense to the brigades and the OZ when he says that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what Siljeg actually meant. You're asking me for my opinion and not Siljeg's opinion, so I don't really know. It would have been far better had you put these documents to General Petkovic and possibly Colonel Siljeg. But as you are asking me I am giving my own opinion. I can't say what Siljeg meant and thought without specifying any documents. You're asking me, I'm giving you my answers, but I can't interpret everything. I can only speculate because I wasn't there or it was -- you're showing me a document that was written when I wasn't down there, a document that I didn't sign. But since you're asking me I'm going to answer to the best of my abilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I haven't prepared the document but I have shown it a number of times. I know its number, so may we pull it up on e-court to avoid any misunderstanding linked to Mr. Siljeg. It is document 5D00538. It's already been exhibit. I have shown it in this courtroom at least ten times already, and it is the minutes from the coordination session with the commanders of the operation zone of western Herzegovina, and the minutes are signed once again by Mr. Siljeg. It was sent to all the units in the operations zone, the defence administration, Tomislavgrad, the Main Staff, HVO, Defence Department. The date of the document is the 9th of March, 1993, and let's look at point number 1. And it's on page 2 of the Croatian and on page 2 of the English, and the title there is: "Point 1," that's what that whole section is called, "Item 1." And I'm reading the second sentence: "According to the plan of the organisation and establishment structure of the OZ S/Z H, the 2nd Military Police Battalion in this operation zone is -- in this Operations Zone is also under its command, and the supply, formation, and training is carried out by the military police administration." Now, Mr. Siljeg goes on to speak about the brigades and so on, but I'm not going to deal with that. I'm going to move on to the next paragraph and I'm going to begin with the second sentence there too. "The battalion -- military police battalion commanders in executing their military police duties are directly subordinated to the commander of the operations zone ..." And the last sentence reads: "When engaging the military police, the commander of the operations zone shall inform the chief of the military police administration, and when the military police is engaged by the brigade commander, he informs the military police battalion commander and the operations zone commander." Mr. Praljak, yesterday we saw how the military police was established, and then we read out what Mr. Siljeg says about that establishment. And it seems to me that the interpretation given with respect to coordination was identical to what we were able to read in the document on military police establishment?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but by your leave I would like to object to this question. I believe that this is a misleading question because we skipped the first page of this document, which clearly indicates that this is a coordination meeting attended by the representatives of the Main Staff and the representatives of the military police, and that at that meeting there is a discussion about the organisation and work of the military police, and then the participation in this discussion on the part of Mr. Siljeg is now attempted to be misrepresented as a conclusion about what the military police is supposed to do in an operational zone. So could we please just explain the actual nature of this document and to show that these are just minutes from a meeting. Furthermore, it is important that this meeting took place about one month after the previous document that we discussed was issued. So I think that there is a complete confusion, and we will not know what rules were in force. I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- well, I, unlike my colleague, are not aware whether this is a discussion or a conclusion because this is not clearly indicated in the document and I would like to ask my learned friend from refrain from commenting on documents. The Judges can read the document. They are here to check whether I am reading something incorrectly. And Mr. Praljak, if he is not familiar with it, is free to say that he's not and to tell me that he did not attend the meeting and that he doesn't know whether this is a conclusion or something else. I have shown this document a number of times, and the only reason why I show it is to establish a link with the previous document and to indicate the three documents, the establishment of the military police, the order by Mr. Siljeg, and this coordination are not mutually exclusive but in fact are linked and point to each other. This was my intention but I am not claiming now what exactly is it that Mr. Siljeg says, whether this is a conclusion, because I cannot see it from the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I really do apologise, Mr. Praljak, you did not answer my question and I don't know whether you know what the question was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer your question. In the document about the structure of the military police you skipped an item where it says that the military police is under the command of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not skip it, I read it out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the military police administration commands, organises, pays, appoints people, and receives reports from the military police. It is true that there are problems. Well, the essence of this meeting and everybody actually received reports about it. This is Mr. Siljeg's opinion and he was a military police officer in the JNA. So he favoured the structure of the military police as it was in the JNA, but in the HVO we did not want to do it like that. So the essence lies in the following paragraph. So what does the military police do and whether it is doing its job properly, and that means whether the military police administration is doing its job properly. Let me quote: "At the meeting various cases were presented" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] " ... murders --" Let me quote slowly this time. "Various cases were presented at the meeting, murders, robberies --" MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm sorry, I have to interrupt. What I want to know is whether you attended the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why are you asking me about a meeting that I wasn't? Why are you showing me a document. So you want to show me parts of the document to confirm your argument, and I don't want to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You don't want to confirm it. Let us move on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please answer the questions asked by counsel, but you actually already said it and I think it's important what you just said, but very briefly it might have failed to the he notice of everyone, maybe not but you never know. You said that Mr. Siljeg was part of the military police of the JNA and he knew the system very well so this is an item of information that you've provided us with. Secondly, you said, We wanted to act differently. When you said that, I thought of what you said previously and from what I understood you said, Within the HVO we wanted to control brigade commanders, and by doing so we were asking the SIS and the military police to play a different role, which means that they were going to control what brigade commanders were going to do. And that was not the case within the JNA, within the JNA as far as I can understand what you're trying to say to us, the military police was subordinated to the brigade commander, and you are saying that in the HVO system the military police was actually reporting or was under the authority of the police administration department, therefore, the Defence Department. And this is obviously something that is very important and that you seem to have brought alight. Am I correct, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. In the Yugoslav People's Army, the military police was subordinate in all its elements to the commanders of units at certain levels, and the Croatian army and the HVO wanted to set up a system, whereby the commander of a brigade or an operational zone or the Main Staff, indeed, does not appoint the chief of the military police or the commanders of battalions. They are not part of the same structure. And this made it possible for the brigade commander or operational zone commander to control whether the military police is doing its job and to ask them to do their job, but the military police has its own structure because the zone commander did not appoint the commander of the military police. So the military police commander cannot be prevented or prohibited by the operational zone commander to report that the operational zone commander or the brigade commander are not doing their job properly, and the same went for the SIS. The SIS did its job as part of the brigade, but it had a chain of command going up to say that the brigade commander is not doing his job properly, is not punishing his troops and so on. It is a democratic structure in an army set-up in this manner, creating parallel structures by way of having checks and balances so that you don't have a system where one person controls everything. So that's the gist of the whole story, and the military police and the SIS have to do their job, and the brigade commander and the operational zone commander can tell them, Do your job, and in this item which I cannot read it is quite clearly stated why the meeting was convened and what the problems were. And, of course, Siljeg and partly Blaskic, who came from the JNA, we had the same problem in the HVO, they were inclined to have the same system that they had come from, but those were their opinions and they sent this to this address and I don't think that it was actually adopted. Nobody adopted it. It's their opinion but it was not translated into any kind of structure. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, to be quite specific, you spoke about how decisions were made as to what the jurisdiction of the military police would be and you said "we in the HVO thought," who are the "we"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, so this is what is on paper. That's the structure as it was established in the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the way I understood it -- well, it's them then, not us, because you are not in this structure that you listed, you're not among the names that you've just given us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Praljak, tell me, did you take part in the drafting of the structure or establishment of the HVO military police, the document that we looked at signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I did participate in Zagreb and it was more or less copy pasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, when was the first time that you read the establishment of the military police of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that I took part of it in Zagreb, and I knew that, and I tell you that it was mostly copy pasted from the HV into HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No that was not my question. My question was when was the first time that you read this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you read it before you took up your post or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, definitely before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Praljak, I failed to understand how is it -- well, did you, when you went to see Mr. Boban, did you discuss it? Why did you go to Mr. Boban when under the establishment as we can see here you had the right to use the military police even without asking Mr. Boban to approve it? You don't have to raise my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If something is being put to the witness it should be put to the witness correctly. General Praljak took up his post on the 24th of July, 1993. Before that there was a restructuring of the military police, and from that time on the system in place was completely different than the one that existed in 1992. So I would like it to be put to him in this way. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I will ask Mr. Praljak since he read the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the restructuring of the military police done immediately before your arrival and what actually changed, the restructuring that my colleague Ms. Pinter has just referred to? It is true that the military police was restructured, and I would like to know what essential changes were carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to do a parallel analysis or a comparison, you have to give me both documents. Now you expect me to provide you an answer 18 years after the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, here in the courtroom you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the phase of cross-examination is a tricky one indeed, and Mr. Stringer is going to ask you questions and this will also be very tricky and difficult, so you have to keep cool, you have to listen carefully to the questions that are put to you, take time before you answer, and try and answer calmly. I know that it is very difficult sometimes, sometimes I also lose my cool. I'm trying to be disciplined, and I believe that this is something that we all have to abide by. So please listen carefully to what the counsel is putting to you. She is doing her job because she's defending Mr. Coric's interests, and so she's checking with you some parts of her case. You have said please show me the documents because 18 years later I do not have them in mind, and I agree with you. But regardless of that, perhaps if you can try and recollect the main lines of the restructuring if you can recollect; if not, if it's too complicated, say so and say you cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I remembered the basic tenets of the establishment. The reason is my demand to Mr. Boban with the approval by Mr. Stojic -- well, in fact, the knowledge of the establishment and the demand to be given the right to exercise operational control over the police -- or rather, to use them in operational terms. The reason -- well, they signed the document and it is quite logical to assume that before that I did not have that right or that right did not not exist because otherwise they would have told me, Well we don't have to sign anything. We do not have to subordinate them to you operationally, I mean the military police, because under the establishment you have the right to do it anyway. So that's my answer, and, Your Honour, I know that there would be questions -- there will be questions, but I have no problems because I know what I know. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the reason why I did not present it and why I thought I would not have to prepare this document about the re-establishment or restructuring is because on several occasions in the course of your examination you spoke about the establishment of the military police with quite some certainty, to whom it was subordinate, and in what manner, and you were shown documents regarding the establishment, and you acted as if you have full knowledge of the area.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just a moment, I'm waiting for the transcript, and to be quite frank, since you are an HVO general, I expect you to be very well acquainted with the establishment of the HVO military police, and I do not expect that I would have to show you in your capacity as the HVO general the documents that applied at the time while you were the commander of the Main Staff. That's all. I didn't want to mislead you. I simply wanted to tell you that. Let us move on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, you can't say something without allowing me to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, because I didn't ask you. I merely stated the fact that the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel and witness are kindly asked not to speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please wait. First of all, Mr. Praljak, wait until the counsel has finished with her question before you answer in order to avoid having voices overlapping on the transcript. From a technical point of view the counsel, and rightly so, said that she thought you knew everything about military police until now because you answered to all the previous questions without any problems. And therefore she's explaining to you why he she didn't deem it necessary to include in the binder or to show all the documents regarding to the military police because she felt that you were aware of all that. You just said that there are things that you were aware of and others that you were not aware of. Now, if Mr. Coric's counsel wants to go in depth, she can ask her co-counsel to dig up the documents and to show them to us. Ms. Tomic, please proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I ask you to look at document 5D04040, 5D04040. This is a document drafted by Mr. Blaskic. I remember that yesterday you said that the operational zone of Central Bosnia was in specific circumstances and that Mr. Blaskic had rights that were not enjoyed by others, but the reason why -- well, I will show you some documents drafted by Mr. Blaskic after documents that were drafted by Mr. Siljeg. And the reason is because I want to compare whether they say the same thing in principle. This is a document of the 6th of May, 1993. It was sent to the commander of the Travnik Brigade and to the commander of the 4th Battalion of the HVO military police in Vitez. The subject is: "Activity of the MP Unit Attached to the Command of the HVO Travnicka Brigade - order." And Mr. Blaskic says as follows: "Based on the evaluation and the analysis of the actual status of the operation of the HVO military police unit and in order to ensure further execution of the tasks --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French interpreters are no longer interpreting. There must be a problem with the interpretation. Please resume. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Based on an evaluation and an insight into the factual circumstances prevailing in the MP HVO and with the objective of furthering the functional performance of the task of the MP HVO, I hereby order: "1. All MP HVO units in the zone of responsibility of the brigade commander are subordinated in the sense of their functional use, control and command, to the brigade commander. "2. The brigade platoon of the MP HVO of the Travnik Brigade shall perform military police tasks in compliance with any orders issued by the commander of the Travnik Brigade and for the needs of that brigade alone. "3. The platoon of the regional MP shall perform tasks on KP ..." And then three check-points, "KP" stands for check-point. Mr. Praljak, in terms of its intention and in terms of what it says about exercising command over the military police and military police tasks, they're talking about the regional platoon and the platoon of the military police and all the platoons of the military police, is this order equivalent to all the documents by Mr. Siljeg that we've been looking at from the south-western Herzegovina operations zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the powers assumed by Mr. Blaskic here are greater. He's talking about functional use. He must mean operational or operative use. This may have to do with conveying Blaskic's request or appeal from the spring of 1993. It's what I conveyed to Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next document, 5D04030. Again, a document by Mr. Blaskic, the 14th of May, 1993. Issues an order to the brigade commander from Kiseljak and says: "Due to a need for a unilateral activity by the forces of the civilian and military police in your zone of responsibility, it is your responsibility to act in compliance with item 7 of the referenced order, saying that all police forces, both military and civilian, shall be placed under the commander of the Ban Jelacic brigade commander. "All civilian and military police commanders shall be informed of this." My question is the same as the one in relation to the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite obvious that Blaskic is here exercising the powers that he received from Boban. There is no other way to interpret this. At this point in time Blaskic is entirely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This has -- thank you. This has not been translated, the last sentences, because you have again overlapped. So you should go back and take up -- but while I have interrupted anyway I read: "Due to the need of unilateral activity of the civil and military police force ..." This doesn't make much sense to me. I do not understand it. Should it perhaps be "coordinated" or something in that sense? Perhaps that could be clarified. It's a linguistic problem, really. Thank you. You may continue. Perhaps you put your question again, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document reads: "Due to a need for a unilateral activity ..." Were I to explain what I believe Mr. Blaskic meant, I think I'd be testifying myself which would not be all right. The only thing I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not ask you for more than the sheer linguistic explanation. So maybe, Mr. Praljak, do you know what that is supposed to mean, what Tihomir Blaskic wants to say when he asks for unilateral activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all likelihood he meant acting together, acting in concert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I see you have the same explanation that I have proposed. Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you obviously disagree with Ms. -- Mr. Coric's counsel. This is really obvious. This document we have written by Mr. Blaskic, as well as all the other ones we saw before, are quite straightforward. He is placing the military police under the authority of the brigade commander. Now, you told us and you explained, number one, that Mr. Blaskic was in direct relationship with Mate Boban; secondly, that Mr. Blaskic was encircled and that Kiseljak was also a pocket, and this might explain several things; but then there could also be another situation that you are not referring to which is in line with the case that you put forth, control by the SIS of military -- of brigade commanders, that Mr. Blaskic would be in total disagreement with this situation because he's an ex-JNA officer, he was trained according to Yugoslav practices, and he believes that the military police must depend -- must be subordinated to the brigade commander. And then in May we are not number one, number one is Mr. Petkovic at the time. You came from the Republic of Croatia. You were volunteered from the Republic of Croatia. That's what you told us. Now maybe your own idea of the thing, which was a Croatian idea, coming from the Republic of Croatia, it might not have been shared by the Croats who lived in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so against your own ideas some people actually issued orders that were counter to what you believed. Is this completely irrealistic [as interpreted], is this assumption irrealistic according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is simply not right. The structural documents clearly indicate what powers belonged to who, and one should work like that in keeping with that structure. I'm not saying anything because sometimes the roads were blocked and a war was on, sometimes one could not have a proper structural procedure, and sometimes orders could not be issued that had gone through the proper procedure. And I myself did that at times because the damage caused by waiting for a full procedure to take place would have been immense. It's simply how it works on the ground, and each commander has the right and duty to act in a way that he believes would cause the least damage. This does, however, amount to bypassing the proper system.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would like to skip a couple of documents now. I see that I'm proceeding at a very slow pace, therefore my next document will be -- just a minute, please. We'll be skipping the rest of Central Bosnia without -- oh, right, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, about the transcript, the interpreter tells us here that he did not hear the last sentence and we were about to place this same remark on the transcript. Praljak finished by saying something else. He said, This means bypassing the existing system, and I won't testify on his behalf. I think he should be asked to repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bypassing a system at one point in time is not tantamount to changing this same system. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be skipping the next eight documents on Central Bosnia because I believe that Mr. Praljak will be providing the same answer to each and every one of these documents, so we're moving on to P01272.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far what my documents have shown is what sort of commander there was over the military police and their military police tasks on a daily basis across two operations zones. Now we're about to move on to the third operations zone, south-east Herzegovina. We'll be looking at P01272. I believe we've got it already. The date is the 23rd of January, 1993. This is an order by the commander of the south-east Herzegovina operations zone, Mr. Lasic. We see that it was distributed to the 3rd Military Police Battalion, a number of brigades, and a number of other units as well. Let's see what paragraph 1 says just underneath where it says "order." "I hereby ban from entering the area of Mostar municipality as well as the remaining municipalities of the south-east Herzegovina operations zone all persons who do not have an official residence anywhere in these municipalities." And now let us skip to the end of that document where Mr. Lasic says: "The following persons shall be responsible for the implementation of this order: The 3rd Battalion of the military police of the HZ HB and the unit commands. The passage of the international humanitarian convoys through the south-east Herzegovina operations zone will be regulated and monitored by the HVO's military police." Mr. Praljak, what about this order by Mr. Lasic, is it not in reference to military police jobs and duties as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be skipping another document here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, your -- the counsel's question was quite broad. She is asking you whether this document has to do with the working of the military police and you're saying yes. But maybe you haven't read the order in its totality, which I just did. When you look at the document as a whole you note that Mr. Milenko Lasic is talking about the unfolding situation, unfolding after what happened in Gornji Vakuf, and is requesting the military police to establish check-points, to seize weapons, and to regulate the passage of international convoys. What is he asking exactly in a nutshell? He's asking the military police to do its basic job, which is to control traffic. Is this what this document states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, of course I read the document, but the only thing I can possibly respond to is the question as asked. Milenko Lasic tells the military police to do their job. The job is defined by the job description. It would have been great for Valentin Coric to have been there with him to issue this order together; nevertheless, it's Milenko Lasic facing this problem and he is here telling the military police to do their job. He is the one facing the problem and he is the one dealing with it by appealing to all the various structures to continue to do their job. He's telling them to do their job. It doesn't mean that he is necessarily in charge of those bodies and structures. We can talk on about this until the end of time, it won't change anything; I stick by my view and I know exactly how this worked on the ground. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I think a policeman, a military police policeman, at a check-point could not possibly have known that Mr. Lasic was banning anyone from entering the area until the officer eventually received this order. It wasn't before they received this order that anyone was being banned from entering the area, that this officer could possibly have known that he was indeed supposed to stop people from entering, those who were banned. How could he possibly have done this job without receiving the order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but at his check-point -- while he was at the check-point determined by the military police and chief of the military police, the policemen of theirs, but they have to fulfil, quite obviously -- or, rather, deal with the problem of people coming into Mostar in an uncontrolled fashion. And then they go on to do the things that Milenko Lasic refers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Praljak. Let's move on to the next document which is -- or actually, we can skip the next document and move on to -- just let me take a moment to find the number. Well, we're going to skip two documents and move on to document number 3 in the series, which is 5D03046. It is a document from Mr. Bozo Pavlovic who was the commander of the Stolac forward command post, as far as I know, and this document is dated the 15th of April. Ms. Alaburic is shaking her head, if there's a problem. No there isn't? Right. Fine. Then we can move on. Anyway, Mr. Pavlovic is the commander here and he's issuing an order under. Under point 1 that: "All vehicles with BH Army insignia markings be prevented from progressing beyond the checkpoints." And then he goes on to enumerate which ones. And then in point 4 he says: "All those who oppose this order shall be disarmed and taken into custody to the Grabovina barracks." The document was sent to the military police, and I think the second PS means "police station." Tell me, Mr. Praljak, does this document also relate to the regular tasks that the military police perform?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a regular task, a regular duty, and except for the announced BH Army vehicles that are due in, everything else should be done according to this order because we're dealing with the 15th of April, and quite obviously the command already has information about the preparations underway in the BH Army for attacking the HVO. So he's still not raising tensions, but he's also securing his back and ensuring that the BH army does not attack and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just waiting for the transcript. Now let's take a look at the next document which is 5D04392. This is once again from Commander Pavlovic dated the 3rd of July, 1993, in which pursuant to an order from the commander of the 1st Knez Domagoj HVO Brigade is issuing this subsequent order to members of the military police, all personnel of the civilian police, and all other soldiers assisting in manning the check-points in the area of responsibility of the Stolac forward command post to prevent any theft of all movable and immovable properties, such as military equipment and weapons. And he goes on to say that you are required regularly to log all confiscated goods and hold them at the check-point and imprison those who violate this order. And we see that this was sent to the military police and also to the civilian police. Tell us now, please, Mr. Praljak, is this another document related to military police affairs and duties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the civilian and military police units and in all the other documents, the commanders are actually saying, You're not doing your job properly, and, Go ahead and do your job properly. That's what these orders are about. Commanders have seen that theft is taking place, property being seized, and then he's telling everybody or they're telling everybody to take measures to confiscate goods and apprehend the perpetrators, and that's what a commander does when he sees that the system is breaking down and not working properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, do you know what I'm interesting in here looking at this document, it's this: Apart from the military police and the civilian police, all the other soldiers are mentioned which are at the check-points and manned the check-points. So can you tell me who deploys and distributes the soldiers among the various check-points?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, on the 3rd of July, that means three days after the 30th of June, at that time the BH army was behind the HVO's back --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Who can, without going into the reasons, place soldiers at check-points apart from the military police and the civilian police? Who else could do that? Now you've heard in this courtroom what happened on the 30th of June. I know what you're trying to get at, you're trying to get at the security reasons. But I am asking -- let's say the reason was completely justified, who could do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the area could do that, whether the broader area or the more narrow area, to prevent people from being killed, as happened on the 26th in the rear in Capljina, that is his right but also his duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now let's move on to the next document, Mr. Praljak, which is P03160. 3160, the next document in that set. And it's a document from the commander of Sector South, Mr. Obradovic, sent to the civilian police. It is an order, in fact, according to which the security of Stolac, Capljina, and so on, and their property, the security of citizens and their property was placed in the hands of the civilian police. Everybody can read the document. It speaks for itself. I don't have to read it all out. We're not dealing with the military police here, but I just showed it as an example because you were speaking about crimes and law and order and so on. Were you aware of this situation, although it was before your time, but did you know that the situation was as it is set out here and Mr. Obradovic issued orders of this kind to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that he issued orders of this kind. However, he's asking the civilian police -- well, I don't know what is contentious here. I think it's a good order and illustrates the wish on behalf of the commander -- well, the civilian police has to protect citizens, and if it's not doing that, whoever does do that is welcome and does the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, let's move on to the next document which is P03 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be time for a break. It's 10.30. Let's break for 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let's move on to the next document, which is P03135. It's an order from Commander Colonel Nedeljko Obradovic, he's commander of the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade. The date of the order is the 3rd of July, which means before you took up your duties. And here's what the order says. "Pursuant to the newly arisen situation in the areas of responsibility of the 1st Knez Domagoj HVO Brigade and because of increased crime and irresponsible behaviour on the part of certain commanders and soldiers of the 1st HVO Brigade, and pursuant to the unlimited powers conferred upon me over the civilian and military structures in accordance with the expansion of the area of responsibility, I hereby order ..." I'm not going to read all the points of that order, just some of them starting with number 1. "All theft should be prevented or any other form of appropriation of personal and other property of citizens in our area of responsibility. And arrest the perpetrators and initiate criminal proceedings against them through this command." And item 3 now, please. "Immediately prevent all violent behaviour and possible war crimes by members of the 1st Brigade and units attached to it and other persons who find themselves in the brigade's area of responsibility. Arrest all violent -- bullies, disarm them, and institute criminal proceedings against them through this command." And now item 11 going down the line there, Mr. Obradovic says: "For the -- all commanders shall be responsible to me personally for the execution of this order." Now, Mr. Praljak, my first question to you is this: Did you know about this document, albeit you weren't there at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any remarks to make with respect to Mr. Obradovic's order or to you consider it to be a proper and correct order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that under the given circumstances this is a proper and correct order regardless of the fact that he oversteps his authority as brigade commander by issuing it. I don't know who gave him unlimited authority, as he says here, but it's quite obvious that what he wants to do is to prevent the situation of chaos and all the things that were happening, but it does overstep the powers of a brigade commander. But it's better that he acts this way rather than leaving the situation to deteriorate without taking any steps or only taking steps within his powers and authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let's move on to the next document which is 5D02009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Colonel Obradovic in paragraph 1 and in paragraph 3 states that some proceedings have to be instituted and it has to be looked into by the various line of commands, so it says the military police you have to start some processes and I'm going to send them to the military prosecutor. He may not have been aware at that time of Article 7(3) of this Tribunal, but he's doing everything so that one day he will -- it will not be held against him that he did not take the necessary measures. General Praljak, I asked you a few questions regarding the text on the obligation for the brigade commander to send proceedings to the military prosecutor. I did not have the text of this document before me or I didn't have that in mind, but at the same time I felt that it made sense for a brigade commander giving instructions and to institute proceedings and for those to be sent to the military prosecutor. You said earlier on that the order was adapted to the situation, but you felt that Obradovic went beyond his duty or his role. Are you really sure of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. I don't know who gave him these unlimited powers that are referred to here. Here -- obviously, he commands SIS and so on. So in that sense establishment-wise he should have sent a paper there and a paper here, but he did not overstep his powers as a commander who must react. If he finds himself in a situation where things are happening, he has to act morally and honourably and try and establish law and order at any price. Obradovic was a former JNA officer and he's well-acquainted with the Geneva Conventions and the United Nations Charter and so on and so forth, which he says in item 4. So he is acting according to his powers as a commander, but there's no way he can go through the whole procedure asking permission from SIS and so on and so forth. But what he's saying here is, Let's do our job. I think it's a good order. That's how a commander should act and react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. If you look at the last sentence where it says that all commanders have to be informed as well as soldiers, so this order has to be brought to the attention of each and every soldier. Is it general practice or do you think that Colonel Obradovic wanted to stress on the content of this order and make sure that all soldiers be informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw the Siljeg order a moment ago, Judge Antonetti, where it says photocopy a sufficient number of copies and hand it down to the very last soldier. So it's always a question of informing each and every soldier, telling them that they must not violate the regulations, the laws, the Geneva Conventions, and so on. They wanted to bring it right down to the grass roots and inform each and every soldier, because not every soldier needed to know about orders pertaining to action and operations, but each and every soldier needed to know about this and that was more or less customary. That was what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the first question: Who is competent to set into force the law of war? Normally in times of war certain special legal provisions apply. Who has the power to declare that they shall apply? If you don't know ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This must be done either by Mate Boban or someone at the same level. At any rate, it cannot be Obradovic. He's not at the required level to be able to say martial law shall apply, although obviously he's quite prepared to do something along these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Who else is on the level of Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the military structure is concerned, it could only have been Mate Boban perhaps at the proposal of Bruno Stojic or pursuant to a government decision. I don't know. At any rate, I myself could not have declared martial law or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And second -- last question regarding this document. It is ordered here to group the Muslim population in your zone of responsibility. Can you -- do you understand what exactly is meant, what it means in practice, and what the justification or the motivation for this order is? It's point 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protection, Your Honour. Protection. He says "group and secure." He must protect the men. It is quite obvious that the situation was like that. Some people wearing masks started appearing and a commander would have had no choice there. He realises that the whole thing is going to the dogs in terms of the civilian police. So he now must protect the civilian population and he must secure these men. He has no other choice. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, we shall be dwelling briefly on this document. The President prefaced his question by saying that Mr. Obradovic hereby issued orders to the military police. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who is being held responsible here for carrying out this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All unit commanders. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Can we please go to the previous page, paragraphs 1 and 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, is it not true that neither in paragraph 1 nor in paragraph 3 is there any mention of the SIS or indeed the military police? It simply spells out what is to be done, and afterwards start the appropriate procedure through this command.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it says, but I think that is, as a matter of fact, in reference to both the SIS and the military police. This is something that they must do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Obradovic had in mind. I can only say what I see written here in this order. Let's move on to the next document, please, 5D02009. Again, an order by Mr. Obradovic, 5D02009. The date is the 3rd of July; that's before your time. The title is: "Order Regarding the Restriction of Passage and the Checking of Soldiers at Check-Points Delivered." Mr. Obradovic says: "I hereby order: "1. Every commander of a unit of the exit point from their zone of responsibility further into the territory towards the Neretva River shall set up a check-point of the battalion through which only his own soldiers shall be allowed to pass who are in possession of a written authorisation from him." Paragraph 2 reads: "Commanders of the civilian, active-duty, and brigade police may pass through only those -- or may let through only those soldiers or groups of soldiers who are in possession of written authorisation from the unit commander, and these persons shall be allowed to pass these check-points down further into the territory of the Neretva River." Paragraph 3: "The commanders of the units and police manning the check-points shall be responsible for the implementation of this order." We see that the order was delivered to all units, the commander of the civilian police, and the commander of the Dretelj active police. Mr. Praljak, today at page 32, line 16, you said that the military police administration and its head were in charge of determining the positions of check-points. If we look closely at this document we see that it's actually Mr. Obradovic who determines these locations -- or rather, he orders his own unit commanders to set up check-points. Do you have any explanation for this? And by "this," I mean the discrepancy between what you said and what this document reflects.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic is setting up a check-point deep in his own territory because groups had been infiltrated by the BH Army and they were operating behind the lines. However, as for these check-points deeper into the territory, these exist already, and he tells us that these existing ones further into the area should keep operating. Obviously people were leaving their positions and deserting and he was facing problems such as these. Therefore, he authorises his own military police and everybody else to not let through anyone not bearing a written authorisation from the commander allowing them to leave this territory. That is how I read this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, how far does the territory under any unit commander extend?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's at the commander's discretion, isn't it, and it depends on the situation that a commander is facing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, please, 5D021 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, counsel, Mr. President. Just with respect to this document 5D02009, I think there's a mistake in the English translation, and while we're on it I thought I could raise it to see if I'm right, then we can get the translation corrected. And maybe with counsel's help or the witness's help I'm looking at the preamble which in the English version says: "With the aim of executing the order of the Main Staff HVO that all soldiers-Croatians have to be permanently on the filed," f-i-l-e-d, I think that probably should the word "field," f-i-e-l-d, but I think it's a typo in the English translation; and if so, maybe we can correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that everyone agrees that it was a typo. Please proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, 5D02189, another one that's before your time and again the person involved is Colonel Obradovic. This is an order to obscure roads -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] If my learned friends right in front of me could keep their voices down. I can't even hear myself speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order to secure roads and secure work at check-points. Mr. Obradovic here issues an order. What I want to know about is paragraph 1(e), item e in relation to the military police. It reads: "The Capljina civilian police, the Dretelj active-duty military police, and the command of the Capljina Home Guards: "Under the command of the Capljina civilian police and in coordinated action with the above, as well as the brigade military police, shall secure the following road: Klepci - Tasovcici - up to and including Zitomislici, using the existing check-points. Also leave the stronger check-point at Pocitelj. "Along the remaining part of the road, every 800 metres, post a group of five to six men for security purposes." Paragraph 4: "The commanders of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd" and so on, he now enumerates the commanders, "shall be responsible for implementing this order." The list includes the commander of the Dretelj active-duty military police. Mr. Praljak, this is yet another document where we witness Mr. Obradovic, in this case Mr. Obradovic personally issues an order as to where a check-point could be set up. Can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. While using the existing check-points, and given the situation that he now found himself in where at one time 26 of his men had been killed behind the lines, massacred due to the treason of the Muslims within the HVO, and the entirely uncertain situation that prevailed behind the lines along the entire front line, this document is perfectly proper given the context. All he's saying here is telling everyone to do their job because he was in a position where he had no choice but to put in a fast reaction, a dreadfully fast reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to using the existing check-points, he also says here that a check-point is to be set up at Pocitelj; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have two questions on this document. First there's something I'm not too sure about. Regarding Capljina it seems that the entire set-up is placed under the command of the civilian police. So if we understand this correctly there will be check-points with mixed controls, but it's the military police that's in control and commanding. Is this routine or is there a special reason for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this wasn't something that was routine. This document shows exactly a situation where a system has to be bypassed. The date is the 30th of June and that's what makes the document comprehensible. I'm not again going into what happened on the 30th of June. I found out at a later stage based on documents and stories I heard from people. At one point in time, you will remember 26 HVO soldiers deep in the territory behind the lines near Capljina just across from the Neretva River were ambushed and massacred by renegade groups of Muslims who were part of the HVO. Back then one had no idea how many of those groups were around. They were wearing uniforms and could in no way be distinguished from everyone else. It's not like their skin was of a different colour. They were people with all the same features. No racial distinction. They were armed, they were in HVO uniforms, and poised to massacre everyone behind the lines. There was this one single incident in which they killed 25 or 26 men. So that's what we see reflected in this order. He's setting up check-points here at 800-metre intervals with armed men so that they could put up a fight. That’s your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the end of your answer you were pre-empting my second question. When looking at this document we see that there are four battalions who are on the field, they're deployed on the field, and what's interesting is he's asking for small groups of five to six soldiers to be set up, placed every 800 metres. Basically, the armed forces seem to be deployed on the field with six soldiers every 800 metres. This is very far from a traditional check-point where you check the traffic. Here, obviously this operation is meant to secure the field. So this securing operation associating civilian and military police must also involve soldier. There's not enough military policemen to be deployed every 800 metres; right? Do you agree, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Entirely, Your Honour, yes. This is about securing the terrain against infiltrated terror groups. You remember the situation in which I was looking for hunters, local hunters to give us a hand because we didn't have enough military police or civilian police to cover the entire area. So I asked the local hunters to join us. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next one up P02836. Thank you. This is a document by Battalion Commander Mijat Tomic. This is part of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade. The date is the 18th of June, 1993. It's addressed to the Jablanica HVO military police. In this document we see this battalion commander issued the following order: "The Jablanica HVO military police shall set up a check-point at Sovicka Vrata where it will check passing traffic and people" and then there's a bit that's illegible, "to members of the military police. The check-point will be secured by ten soldiers from the battalion." Paragraph 2 reads: "Set up a check-point along the Risovac-Kuharnica road" I'm not sure the place name is correct. It's difficult to read.
